title: HTTP Request/Response, Headers and Cookies: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on the HTTP request/response cycle, methods, headers and status codes, then cookies: the Set-Cookie attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path) and how browsers decide which cookies to attach to a request.

chapters.title: HTTP Mental Model and Request/Response Flow
points: HTTP is a stateless, text-based request/response protocol: the client sends one request, the server returns one response, and the server keeps no memory between requests
Request anatomy: request line (METHOD /path?query HTTP/1.1), then headers, a blank line, then an optional body
Response anatomy: status line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK), then headers, a blank line, then an optional body
Flow for a page load: DNS lookup, TCP + TLS handshake, send request, receive response, browser parses HTML and fires further requests for CSS, JS and images
Statelessness is why sessions exist: the server hands out an ID via Set-Cookie and the client sends it back on every request via Cookie

chapters.title: HTTP Methods and Idempotency
points: GET reads a resource and has no body; POST creates or triggers an action; PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH changes part of it; DELETE removes it
Safe methods change no server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
Idempotent methods give the same end state when repeated: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed idempotent
Comparison PUT vs PATCH: PUT sends the full representation and overwrites it; PATCH sends only the changed fields
OPTIONS is used for CORS preflight and asks which methods and headers the server allows; HEAD returns the headers of a GET with no body
Mistake: using GET for state-changing actions, since prefetchers, crawlers and caches can fire GET requests without user intent

chapters.title: Headers and Status Codes
points: Request headers: Host (required in HTTP/1.1), User-Agent, Accept, Authorization: Bearer <token>, Cookie, Origin
Body headers: Content-Type says what the body is (application/json), Content-Length says its size in bytes
Response headers: Set-Cookie, Location (used with redirects), Cache-Control, Content-Type, Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Status classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
Key success and redirect codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 301 permanent redirect, 302 temporary redirect, 304 Not Modified
Key error codes: 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 authenticated but forbidden, 404 not found, 429 rate limited, 500 server bug, 502/503/504 gateway or upstream failure

chapters.title: Cookies and Their Attributes
points: A cookie is set by the server with Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; the browser stores it and returns it in a Cookie: sid=abc123 header
Secure: the cookie is only sent over HTTPS, so it is never exposed on plain HTTP connections
HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read the cookie through document.cookie, which limits token theft via XSS; the browser still sends it with requests

SameSite: Strict never sends the cookie on cross-site requests; Lax (the browser default) sends it on top-level GET navigations only; None sends it cross-site and requires Secure; SameSite is the main defence against CSRF
Domain: if set, the cookie is also sent to all subdomains (Domain=example.com covers api.example.com); if omitted, it is host-only and goes to that exact host
Path: the cookie is sent only for URLs under that path prefix (Path=/admin); it is not a security boundary, since other paths can still read it from JS on the same origin

Lifetime: with no Expires or Max-Age it is a session cookie that vanishes when the browser session ends; Max-Age=3600 sets seconds to live and takes precedence over Expires; Max-Age=0 deletes the cookie

chapters.title: How Browsers Attach Cookies and Common Mistakes
points: Attach rule: for each outgoing request the browser sends every stored cookie whose Domain matches the host, whose Path is a prefix of the URL path, that is not expired, and that passes the Secure and SameSite checks
Same-site is decided by the registrable domain (eTLD+1) and ignores port, so app.example.com and api.example.com are same-site, while example.com and example.org are cross-site
Cross-origin fetch does not send cookies by default; it needs credentials: 'include' on the client and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with a specific origin (not *) on the server
Mistake: SameSite=None without Secure is rejected by the browser, so the cookie is silently dropped
Mistake: storing session or auth tokens in a cookie without HttpOnly, or in localStorage, which exposes them to XSS
Mistake: changing a cookie's Domain or Path when overwriting or deleting it; a cookie is identified by name + Domain + Path, so a mismatch creates a second cookie instead of replacing the first

chapters.title: HTTP and Cookies Cheat Sheet
points: Methods: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove; safe = GET/HEAD/OPTIONS; idempotent = safe + PUT/DELETE
Status: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client fault, 5xx server fault; 401 means not logged in, 403 means not allowed
Set-Cookie template: name=value; Path=/; Domain=example.com; Max-Age=3600; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Auth session cookie default: Secure + HttpOnly + SameSite=Lax (or Strict) and a short Max-Age
Cross-site cookie needs SameSite=None; Secure, and cross-origin fetch needs credentials: 'include'
Debug: browser DevTools Network tab for the Cookie and Set-Cookie headers, Application tab for stored cookies, and curl -i -b 'sid=abc' https://example.com to replay one
